newsitem.title: USA: Compaq deal seen aiding quest for growth - CEO.
newsitem.headline: Compaq deal seen aiding quest for growth - CEO.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp's $3.0 billion merger with Tandem Computers Inc will help Compaq fill in the missing gaps in its quest to become one of the world's top three computer makers, its CEO said.

Pfeiffer said that Tandem, which develops high-end computer systems for mission critical computing, will double Compaq's current sales force with Tandem's 4,000 member sales team, add a services and support group and technology to help the world's largest PC maker move beyond PCs and PC servers.
"It's a one-stop shopping, total enterprise solution," said Compaq president and CEO Eckhard Pfeiffer, in an interview.
"We need to cover the entire spectrum, software, services and support," Pfeiffer said. "That is the road map to being one of the top three global computer companies."

"We will see very significant revenue growth," Pfeiffer added, but he said he could not be more specific about any financials related to the merger. He said that Compaq decided to use stock instead of cash for the merger so that it would have a "very clean" merger with a pooling of interests.
Compaq will retain its huge cash pile for other uses, including other deals, should they come up, Pfeiffer said but he declined to comment on its other widely-reported merger talks.

"It's all rumors and nothing else," Pfeiffer said. Over the past year, Compaq has been in talks to acquire Digital Equipment Corp, Gateway 2000 Inc and Micron Electronics Inc. Shares of all three companies were off Monday, as traders said any remaining hopes for a deal with Compaq were quashed by its unexpected Tandem merger.

Tandem Computers CEO Roel Pieper said that the deal is a perfect match because Compaq is trying to expand its business to include the corporate enterprise market - the technology that runs the big Fortune 500 companies - and Tandem is expanding its market to include Windows NT-based servers.

"We have been trying to move down into the market and they are trying to move up into the market," Pieper said. "A company that wants to win needs to have both...so a customer has a one-stop shopping solution (for) all the things they need.""

Tandem and Compaq and Microsoft Corp have already been working together developing "clustering" technology, which lets multiple processors grouped together vastly improve system performance on systems running Windows NT software.
But Tandem's core business, or about 70 percent of its revenues, are from its "fault-tolerant" systems that never fail developed around its proprietary architecture.
